OUTLINE VIEW

Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the pathoanatomy associated with physeal fractures of the distal femur and their
associated complications.
Formulate a treatment plan for the management of physeal fractures of the distal femur.
Predict and manage complications associated with physeal fractures of the distal femur.
Overview
A physeal fracture of the distal femur should be considered in children who have knee pain
after trauma (with or without deformity), swelling, and limited ability to bear weight. Physeal
fractures of the distal femur are notorious for subsequent physeal arrest. Therefore, treating
physicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for this injury and, after diagnosis and
acute treatment, monitor patients for impending or resultant limb abnormalities.

Anatomy, Biomechanics, and Mechanism of Injury
The physis of the distal femur is responsible for approximately 70% of longitudinal femoral
growth.
The undulating pattern of the distal femoral physis contributes to an increased risk of physeal
arrest after injury.
In the pediatric knee, varus or valgus force leads to physeal disruption of the distal femur (or
proximal tibia) rather than failure of the medial or lateral collateral ligaments, as seen in adults
(Figure 1).
Periosteum may become entrapped within the physeal fracture on the tension side (opposite
the Thurstan-Holland fragment) and prevent closed reduction.
In patients with a severely displaced fracture, the popliteal neurovascular bundle and/or
peroneal nerve are at risk.


Anatomy, Biomechanics, and Mechanism of Injury
Physeal fractures of the distal femur account for approximately 2% of all physeal
fractures. They are most common in juvenile and adolescent patients (mean age, 10 to
13.4 years) and may result from low- or high-energy mechanisms of injury (eg, sports
accidents or vehicular trauma). The medial and collateral ligaments originate on the
epiphysis of the distal femur and resist injury in the pediatric knee better than the
physis. Therefore, a varus or valgus load may lead to failure of the periosteum on the
tension side along with the underlying physis. Fractures irreducible via closed
manipulation may have torn periosteum entrapped on the tension side, necessitating
open reduction. In Salter-Harris type II and type IV fracture patterns, force travels along
the hypertrophic zone and exits the compression side via a metaphyseal fragment
(termed the Thurstan-Holland fragment).
The physis of the distal femur is responsible for approximately 70% of longitudinal
femoral growth.1 In addition, the undulating pattern of the physis of the distal femur
makes it particularly susceptible to permanent arrest.2 The physis is more linear along
its anterior aspect and concave in the posterior portions of the medial and lateral
femoral condyles.3 Lateral radiographs of the knee may not afford visualization of these
undulations perfectly; therefore, care should be taken to avoid iatrogenic injury during
fixation.4
Similar to adult distal femur fractures and knee dislocations, the popliteal neurovascular
structures and the peroneal nerve are at risk. The gastrocnemius can flex the distal
fragment, and the hamstrings and extensor muscles of the thigh can shorten the
fracture site.

Injury Classification
The Salter-Harris classification system is used to describe physeal fractures of the distal femur.
Salter-Harris type II fractures are most common.

Injury Classification
In a meta-analysis of 11 studies (n = 485), the prevalence of physeal fractures of the
distal femur according to the Salter-Harris classification system was as follows: type I,
14%; type II, 57%; type III, 10%; type IV, 12%; and type V, 3%. 5
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with a nondisplaced fracture will present with a history of trauma to the knee, focal
tenderness, swelling, and limited ability to bear weight.
Patients with a displaced fracture often have gross deformity.
A neurovascular examination is important to rule out acute injury to the popliteal artery.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with a nondisplaced injury (especially those in whom radiographs appear
normal) should be examined for focal tenderness, swelling, and limited ability to bear
weight, with a high index of suspicion maintained for physeal injury of the distal femur.
Patients with a displaced injury should undergo a detailed neurovascular examination,
with emphasis on the popliteal neurovascular bundle and the peroneal nerve. An ankle-
brachial index of less than 0.9 is an indication for Doppler or CT angiography.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are adequate if the fracture is visualized; however, radiographs also may be
unremarkable.

If plain radiographs are unremarkable or insufficient to guide treatment decisions, then CT or
MRI is appropriate.

Imaging Studies
Although often sufficient, plain radiographs of the knee may be unremarkable in
patients with a minimally displaced fracture or may demonstrate a small metaphyseal
fleck or subtle physeal widening. Stress radiographs, with or without sedation, are no
longer recommended because of patient discomfort and unnecessary manipulation of
an at-risk physis.6 CT or MRI is appropriate if plain radiographs are inconclusive, the
fracture involves the articular surface, or additional fracture characterization will aid in
preoperative planning. In patients with a Salter-Harris type III fracture, radiographs often
underestimate displacement; therefore, CT or MRI is indicated.7
Management
Fractures that are not displaced on presentation can be managed via immobilization if close
follow-up to monitor for early displacement is possible.
Due to high rates of early displacement, patients with a minimally displaced (<2 mm) fracture
(especially Salter-Harris type III/type IV fractures through the weight-bearing articular surface)
are candidates for prophylactic fixation.
Displaced fractures (>2 mm) should be managed via closed versus open reduction and
fixation.
Patients should be monitored after healing for physeal arrest. (Resource 1).
Nonsurgical Management
Minimally displaced (<2 mm) fractures can be managed nonsurgically, with close follow-up to
rule out early displacement.
The best candidates for nonsurgical treatment are patients with a Salter-Harris type I/type II
fracture that is nondisplaced (based on CT or MRI).


Nonsurgical Management
Minimally displaced fractures that do not require a closed reduction can be considered
stable enough to initiate treatment in a long leg cast. Early follow-up radiographs are
necessary to rule out interval displacement. The status of the physis should be
monitored for arrest because growth disturbance can still occur in patients with a
nondisplaced fracture (Figure 2).

was brought to the hospital by his elderly caretaker with a right knee effusion 1 week
after being struck by a car. Initial AP (A) and lateral (B) right knee radiographs were

Salter-Harris type II physeal fracture of the distal femur (arrow) that was managed via a
long leg cast. The patient was briefly lost to follow-up. On return to the clinic, a full-

Surgical Management
Initially displaced (>2 mm) Salter-Harris type I/type II fractures and all Salter-Harris type III/type
IV fractures should be managed via surgical fixation.

Surgical Management
Initially displaced (>2 mm) Salter-Harris type I/type II fractures and all Salter-Harris type
III/type IV fractures are ideal candidates for surgical fixation due to high rates of
displacement during nonsurgical management.8,9 Inability to obtain acceptable closed
reduction (<2 mm) is also an indication for open reduction. Surgical techniques for
different Salter-Harris fracture patterns vary slightly, with overlapping fixation options.
Salter-Harris type III/type IV fractures are immediate candidates for open reduction and
fixation because radiographs and intraoperative fluoroscopy often underestimate true
articular displacement. Many authors recommend a mini-arthrotomy to palpate or
visualize articular congruity during fixation.7
Techniques/Procedures
Closed reduction usually is possible in patients with a Salter-Harris type I/type II fracture.
If the physis is irreducible via closed means, then open reduction and removal of entrapped
periosteum (on the tension side) is indicated.
In patients with a Salter-Harris type III/type IV fracture involving the weight-bearing articular
surface, fluoroscopy and other methods may underestimate articular displacement,

warranting a mini-arthrotomy to assess reduction during fixation.
Fixation should avoid the physis if possible. If fixation must cross the physis, smooth Kirschner
wires (K-wires; antegrade versus retrograde) are used.

Techniques/Procedures
For Salter-Harris type I/type II fractures, gentle manipulation of the physeal fracture is
usually adequate to achieve closed reduction. Displacement in the sagittal plane often
can be corrected by flexing the knee over a sterile triangle. A varus or valgus force
should reduce coronal plane deformities. The most common impediment to acceptable
closed reduction is torn periosteum entrapped within the tension side of the physis
(Figure 3). If this is suspected, open reduction is indicated. Although surgeons may be
tempted to visualize the metaphyseal Thurstan-Holland fragment (the insertion point for
cannulated screws on the compression side), an open approach should be performed
over the entrapped periosteum on the tension side (opposite the Thurstan-Holland
fragment, the location at which percutaneous cannulated screws can be used; Figure 4).

(Images courtesy of Dustin A. Greenhill, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
After reduction has been achieved, the type of fixation depends on the characteristics of
the fracture and the size of the patient. The physis should be avoided if possible. If a
metaphyseal Thurstan-Holland fragment is large enough to accept screw fixation (as in
many Salter-Harris type II or type IV fractures), percutaneous, partially threaded, 4.5-mm
to 7.3-mm cannulated screws (with or without a washer) are appropriate.
For Salter-Harris type III/type IV fractures with epiphyseal involvement, a single
epiphyseal screw placed within the target triangle is appropriate7 (Figure 5). Special care
should be taken during screw placement to avoid iatrogenic physeal damage of the
posterolateral physeal undulation, which is poorly visualized on lateral radiographs.4 To
palpate or visualize articular reduction, a mini-arthrotomy is advocated in some studies
because persistent displacement has been described via alternative assessment
methods, such as arthrography or arthroscopy.7

If extraphyseal fixation is not possible (eg, Salter-Harris type I fracture) or is insufficient
(eg, fractures with a small or comminuted metaphyseal fragment), large smooth
transphyseal K-wires can be used. These K-wires may contribute to unavoidable physeal
bar formation. The K-wires can be placed antegrade or retrograde, left intracapsular or
within the epiphysis, and left outside or placed underneath the skin (Figure 6). Some
surgeons place pins in a retrograde fashion because it is technically easier but advance
them out the thigh proximally so the hardware is completely within the bone. The risk
associated with proximally located pins with regard to the adductor canal has not been
quantified. Factors that determine K-wire technique include surgeon comfort, pin tract
infection and risk of concomitant septic arthritis with retrograde placement, and ease of
removal at 4 weeks postoperatively.
Figure 6 AP knee radiographs (A and C) and AP knee fluoroscopic image (B) shows
transphyseal fixation with the use of Kirschner wires in various configurations (Panels A
and B courtesy of Dustin A. Greenhill, MD, Philadelphia, PA. Panel C reproduced from
Bassett WP, Safier S, Herman MJ, Kozin SH, Abzug JA: Complications of pediatric femoral
shaft and distal physeal fractures. Instr Course Lect 2015;64:461-470.)
A long leg cast (or a knee immobilizer) should be used for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively,
after which early motion therapy is initiated to avoid arthrofibrosis.

Complications
Distal femur fractures tend to be associated with a worse prognosis than other physeal
fractures, with primary concerns being physeal arrest and pin tract infection.
The risk factors most frequently associated with complications are high-energy mechanism of
injury and initial fracture displacement.
Neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome are rare complications but should be
considered.
Growth arrest occurs in approximately 21% to 52% of patients with a physeal fracture of the
distal femur.
Pin tract infection can be avoided via surgical technique and timely pin removal.
Range of motion should be initiated approximately 4 weeks postoperatively to avoid
arthrofibrosis.

Complications
Distal femur fractures are associated with a high overall complication rate (36% to 40%)
compared with other physeal fractures.10,11 The most common complication is physeal
arrest (21% to 52% per a recent, large series), likely because of the undulating nature of
the distal femoral physis and, its major contribution to longitudinal growth and because
of the age at which these fractures occur. Some studies have reported a higher rate of
complications; however, they also analyzed a larger proportion of severe fractures.
Basener et al5 reported growth arrest in 63% of fractures (19 of 30) that required
fixation. Displacement and a high-energy mechanism of injury are consistently
associated with complications.5, 10-12 Nondisplaced fractures are associated with the
lowest (although not negligible) rate of complications.
Growth arrest is most likely a result of the initial physeal injury because its incidence is
not decreased via reduction or surgical management.10 Acceptable reduction is
associated with optimal outcomes, minimizing ligamentous laxity, avoiding
malalignment, and avoiding posttraumatic arthritis. Standing lower extremity
radiographs should be obtained by 6 to 12 months postinjury and scrutinized for
physeal arrest. If physeal arrest is discovered, then advanced imaging studies should be
obtained and deformity principles should be applied.

Transphyseal K-wires have been associated with pin tract infection and physeal bar
formation. In a retrospective review of 55 patients, Garrett et al12 reported that smooth
transphyseal pins were not statistically associated with growth arrest. However, after
placement of smooth transphyseal pins in 30 rabbits, Dahl et al13 reported a 7%
incidence of small physeal bar formation on cross-sectional imaging studies These
authors concluded that, although adequate fixation is a priority, physeal bar formation
may be unavoidable in certain fracture scenarios.
The ideal entry point and final positioning of K-wires is surgeon dependent. Several
studies advocate antegrade and/or extracapsular placement to limit the risk of septic
arthritis. Although retrograde placement of K-wires (entering the epiphysis extra-
articularly via the lateral condyles) may be technically easier, it is associated with a risk of
joint contamination via pin tract infection. Murgai et al14 supported retrograde K-wire
placement, given the 6.7% rate of pin tract infection (among 142 osteotomies and 21
physeal fractures) and zero patients with septic arthritis reported in the study. Although
not reported, anecdotal cases of septic arthritis after retrograde pin placement exist. In
addition, a more recent series reported a 17% rate of pin tract infection (3 of 18),
whereby two underwent formal irrigation and débridement.10 Pins can be cut under the
skin and removed in the operating room which theoretically decreases the risk of pin site
infection. Pins should be removed 4 weeks postoperatively.
